title: Complications of Neurological Disorders
path: Management of Clients with Neurologic Disorders

headings.title: Introduction and Pathophysiological Overview
headings.content: Neurological disorders frequently trigger secondary cascades that extend far beyond the initial brain or spinal cord insult. When neurons experience trauma, ischemia, or inflammatory injury, local homeostatic mechanisms fail rapidly. This triggers a destructive cycle involving cellular energy depletion, excessive neurotransmitter release, and escalating tissue swelling. Nurses working in Nigerian acute and emergency care settings must recognize that secondary neurological injuries are largely preventable. Vigilant bedside monitoring detects subtle clinical shifts before irreversible tissue destruction occurs. The primary objective in managing complex neurological conditions is safeguarding surviving brain parenchyma and maintaining stable systemic perfusion.

headings.title: Increased Intracranial Pressure and Brain Herniation
headings.content:
The cranium is a rigid box containing brain tissue, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid. According to the Monro-Kellie doctrine, an increase in any one of these components must be offset by a decrease in the others, otherwise intracranial pressure rises. 

- **Early ICP signs**: Decreased level of consciousness, headache, and confusion.
- **Late ICP signs**: Cushing's triad (bradycardia, widening pulse pressure, irregular respirations).
- **Herniation syndromes**: Uncal or central shifting of brain tissue through rigid intracranial folds, leading to brainstem compression and rapid death.

headings.title: Cerebral Edema, Ischemia, and Herniation Risks
headings.content: Cerebral edema is an abnormal accumulation of fluid within the brain parenchyma, categorized primarily as vasogenic or cytotoxic. Vasogenic edema stems from a compromised blood-brain barrier, allowing plasma proteins and fluids to leak into the extracellular space. Cytotoxic edema involves cellular swelling due to hypoxic injury and cellular pump failure. As edema expands, local microvasculature compresses, causing severe ischemia. This lack of oxygen fuels further metabolic acidosis and cell death, creating a vicious feedback loop that precipitates brain herniation.

headings.title: Seizures and Status Epilepticus
headings.content: Uncontrolled electrical discharges in the cerebral cortex can manifest as focal or generalized seizures. When a seizure lasts longer than five minutes or repeats without recovery between episodes, it becomes status epilepticus, a medical emergency. Prolonged seizure activity drastically increases cerebral metabolic demand while reducing oxygen delivery, causing neuronal exhaustion and permanent brain damage. Immediate nursing interventions include maintaining a patent airway, administering prescribed anticonvulsants like diazepam or lorazepam, and monitoring vital signs closely.

headings.title: Autonomic Dysreflexia and Hemodynamic Instability
headings.content: Patients with spinal cord injuries at or above the T6 level are at high risk for autonomic dysreflexia. This life-threatening syndrome is triggered by noxious stimuli below the level of the injury, such as a full bladder, fecal impaction, or tight clothing. Sensory impulses travel up the spinal cord and trigger a massive sympathetic reflex, causing severe vasoconstriction and dangerous hypertension. The parasympathetic system attempts to compensate by slowing the heart rate, resulting in severe throbbing headache, flushing above the injury, and piloerection. Nurses must immediately locate and remove the trigger while managing blood pressure.

headings.title: Impaired Airway Clearance and Aspiration Risks
headings.content: Neurological deficits frequently impair bulbar muscle control, coughing reflexes, and swallowing coordination. Stroke, traumatic brain injury, and advanced neurodegenerative diseases put patients at high risk for silent aspiration and retained pulmonary secretions. When secretions pool in the upper airway or foreign material enters the lungs, chemical pneumonitis and bacterial pneumonia develop rapidly. Regular suctioning, proper positioning, and formal dysphagia screening before oral feeding are core preventative nursing responsibilities.

headings.title: Secondary Systemic Complications: DVT and Pressure Injuries
headings.content: Prolonged immobilization following a neurological insult exposes patients to multiple systemic complications. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) arises from venous stasis in paralyzed or immobile limbs, carrying a high risk for fatal pulmonary embolism. Simultaneously, constant pressure over bony prominences reduces microvascular perfusion, rapidly forming pressure injuries. Nurses combat these risks through scheduled position changes, early mobilization, compression stockings, and meticulous skin hygiene.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Monitoring for Deterioration
headings.content: Early detection of neurological decline requires systematic and frequent clinical evaluations. The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) remains the gold standard for tracking changes in a patient's level of consciousness across eye opening, verbal response, and motor performance. Nurses must also assess pupillary light reflexes, limb strength, and vital sign trends. Any sudden drop in GCS score or asymmetry in pupil reaction demands immediate notification of the medical team.

headings.title: Comprehensive Management and Rehabilitation
headings.content: Managing chronic neurological complications requires a coordinated, multidisciplinary approach involving nurses, physiotherapists, speech therapists, and medical officers. Rehabilitation focuses on maximizing functional independence, preventing joint contractures, and supporting psychological well-being. Nurses play a central role in coordinating care, educating family caregivers on home management, and ensuring continuity from the acute hospital ward back into the community.
